title: Biochemistry practicals
scopeNote: Authored practice from your six local practical stations and saved review. These are not past-paper questions. Lecturer-specific protocols remain named; numerical cases state their own data and are not claimed as your laboratory observations.

stations.title: Safety & laboratory equipment
stations.summary: Choose equipment by what it measures or controls, then identify technique errors before they become analytical errors. The review clarifies precision, centrifuge balancing and safe chemical handling.
checkpoints: A volumetric flask contains one calibrated final volume; a volumetric pipette delivers a fixed calibrated aliquot. A beaker is not precision volumetric glassware.
Read the bottom of a clear aqueous meniscus at eye level; dispense with a pipette aid and obey the delivery markings.
Balance centrifuge tubes by mass in opposite positions; a water bath controls temperature and a fume hood removes hazardous vapours.
Use the local chemical SOP: no mouth pipetting, no ignition source near acetone, and use the eyewash immediately for an eye splash.
traps: A flask marked to contain and a pipette marked to deliver are not interchangeable.
Equipment names alone do not establish safe handling or measurement precision.

stations.title: Titration & equivalent calculations
stations.summary: Calculate the delivered titre before applying equivalent balance. Distinguish the indicator endpoint from the chemical equivalence point, and predict the direction of common burette and dilution errors.
checkpoints: Delivered titre = final burette reading minus initial reading; a nonzero initial reading is not an error if subtracted correctly.
At equivalence, acid normality × acid volume = base normality × base volume. Normality counts reactive equivalents per litre.
The local titrant is 0.1 N NaOH; the endpoint is a faint pink persisting at least 30 seconds after mixing with phenolphthalein.
Add titrant slowly near the endpoint and swirl. Diluting a measured acid aliquot with water does not change its amount of acid.
traps: Endpoint overshoot, an initially air-filled burette tip, and using the final reading alone can overestimate acid normality.
Equivalence does not always mean pH 7, and normality does not always equal molarity.

stations.title: Spectrophotometry & serum protein
stations.summary: Move from light transmission to a defensible concentration result: choose the wavelength, blank correctly, construct standards, check linearity and apply the appropriate calibration or Biuret ratio.
checkpoints: T = I/I₀, A = −log₁₀(T), and %T = 100 × 10^(−A). Absorbance is dimensionless, not the absorbed light intensity I₀ − I.
At fixed wavelength, path length and chemistry, A = εbc. Absorbance is linear with concentration in the valid range; transmittance is not.
The dye experiment uses bromophenol-blue standards prepared from 10 mg/L stock to a final 10 mL, a distilled-water blank, and a 480–620 nm wavelength scan.
The protein protocol uses 0.5 mL sample or 7 g/dL standard plus 2 mL Biuret reagent, a saline blank, 15 minutes at room temperature and measurement at 540 nm.
Protein = Atest/Astandard × 7 g/dL when sample and standard follow the same assay. Apply a separate pre-dilution factor only if the original sample was pre-diluted.
traps: The dye wavelength scan, dye calibration and protein assay are separate experiments; their OD readings are not interchangeable.
A concentration result fixes an OD ratio, not a unique pair of raw readings. Numerical teaching cases are not claimed as student measurements.

stations.title: Amino-acid & protein identification tests
stations.summary: Interpret a pattern of reactions rather than treating any single colour as a complete protein identification. Keep chemical targets, positive appearances, controls and the two lecturer protocols distinct.
checkpoints: Ninhydrin tests free amino groups: most α-amino acids give purple, while proline/hydroxyproline give yellow. Ebrahimi heats 5 minutes; Emamgholipour specifies 10 minutes.
Xanthoproteic nitration gives yellow, enhanced to orange on alkalinisation. Tyr and Trp respond strongly; phenylalanine can respond weakly or negatively under usual conditions.
Pauly detects tyrosine or histidine by red azo coupling; Hopkins–Cole detects the tryptophan indole group as a violet interface.
Qualitative Biuret requires at least two peptide bonds and alkaline Cu²⁺. Denaturation alone need not destroy its peptide-bond response.
TCA precipitates protein: 1+1 mL of protein and 15% TCA in Ebrahimi, versus 2+2 mL in Emamgholipour; both retain a 1:1 volume ratio.
traps: A negative residue-specific test does not prove absence of protein.
Do not merge the ninhydrin heating times or TCA volumes into a nonexistent universal protocol.

stations.title: Enzyme experiments & controls
stations.summary: Read the actual rennin and urease tube plans, identify the variable being changed, and separate expected direction of reaction from measured results. Do not infer a detailed inhibition mechanism from one colour observation.
checkpoints: Rennin/chymosin clots milk; renal renin is a different enzyme. Pre-equilibrate milk and enzyme separately before mixing and starting the timer.
Enzyme-concentration experiment: 2 mL milk with 1, 0.5 or 0.25 mL rennin and enough water to make 3 mL total. More active enzyme generally shortens clotting time.
Substrate experiment: 2, 1 or 0.5 mL milk with compensating water, plus 1 mL rennin in every tube. Dilution changes milk substrate and physical clot formation.
Urease converts urea to ammonia and CO₂; ammonia increases pH, changing phenol red. Compare urea alone, urea plus zinc sulfate, and thiourea under matched conditions.
Temperature and pH affect activity; high temperature can denature enzyme. A fixed-time colour or clot endpoint is not automatically an initial-rate measurement.
traps: The slide’s “renin” spelling does not make the milk-clotting enzyme the renal angiotensinogen-cleaving enzyme.
Reduced colour in zinc sulfate does not prove competitive inhibition, and three milk-clot times do not establish a valid Km.

stations.title: Flame photometry & electrolytes
stations.summary: Understand flame emission and calibration without mistaking visible flame colour for a complete quantitative analysis. The local deck does not supply a full numerical standard-preparation SOP, so the calculation cases state their own teaching data.
checkpoints: Flame photometry detects characteristic light emitted as excited species relax; it is not a measurement of transmitted light through a coloured solution.
Within a validated calibration range, emission intensity can quantify selected elements. Blank, calibrators, quality controls and sample matrix matter.
The local wavelength table lists Na near 589 nm and K near 766 nm. A visually lilac potassium flame is not the same thing as a single violet 766 nm emission line.
mEq/L = mmol/L × absolute ionic charge: monovalent Na⁺/K⁺ retain the number, while Ca²⁺ doubles it.
Electrode methods measure ion activity and can be automated without a flame. Performance depends on method and sample conditions; no universal “ISE is less precise” rule is justified.
traps: A visual flame colour alone is not a concentration measurement or a reliable identification of every component in a mixture.
Do not invent laboratory calibration readings or apply a calibration outside its validated range.
